definition_en: The default Chinese umbrella noun for the post-2022 foundation-model paradigm: any large-scale pretrained model that is adapted to many downstream tasks. It covers LLMs, multimodal and vision-language models, and industry-specific fine-tunes, and is used as a paradigm label rather than a parameter-count threshold — a 4B fine-tune shipped as a product is still 大模型.
definition_zh: 指经大规模数据预训练、可适配多种下游任务的基础模型，是 2022 年以来中文语境中对这一技术范式最通用的称呼。既涵盖通用基础模型，也涵盖垂直行业模型；在中文里它更接近“基础模型/大模型范式”，而不是一个参数量门槛。
pitfalls: 'Large model' is a calque, not idiomatic English — no English-speaking practitioner says it unprompted, yet it is the rendering used in TC260's own official English text and in most translated PRC material, so an English reader meets it constantly. Two specific traps: (1) 大模型 is a paradigm claim, not a size claim, so '大模型' routinely covers models an English writer would call small (Qwen3-4B, industry fine-tunes) — reading it as 'large' imports a false size threshold; (2) it is broader than 'LLM' (it includes multimodal, vision-language-action and diffusion-family models when they are pretrained-and-adapted) but narrower than 'AI model' (a bespoke task-specific classifier is not 大模型). 'Foundation model' is the accurate English concept and 上海AI实验室/安远AI explicitly equate the two, but it is not what translations say. Also note the productive compounds — 大模型备案, 大模型安全, 通用大模型 vs 行业大模型 — which have no single-word English counterparts.

en_renderings.notes: The rendering an English reader will actually meet, including in TC260's own bilingual national framework and in Concordia AI's English reporting. Record it, but it is a calque: it reads as a size adjective in English while the Chinese is a paradigm noun.

why_no_english: English fragmented the concept across three words that Chinese keeps in one. 'LLM' names the modality, 'foundation model' names the training-and-adaptation relationship, and 'frontier model' names the capability tier; 大模型 does all three jobs at once and is the ordinary word a Chinese engineer, journalist, regulator and investor all use. Because English has no single unmarked term, translators fall back on 'large model', which quietly converts a claim about *how a model was built and is used* into a claim about *how big it is* — and so makes PRC statements about small industry models look inconsistent. definition_en: Computational capacity treated as a national resource and a factor of production, on a par with data, energy and land. 算力 is simultaneously the technical quantity English calls 'compute' and the object of a large body of PRC industrial policy — measured in aggregate (EFLOPS), planned by the state, sited by programme (东数西算), and built as 算力基础设施 and 智算中心.
definition_zh: 指计算能力，但在中文政策与产业语境中它同时是一种生产要素和基础设施门类，与数据、能源并列，可统计（EFLOPS）、可规划、可调度，衍生出算力网络、算力中心、智算中心、算力经济等一整套词汇。
pitfalls: English 'compute' is a recent mass-noun back-formation from the AI-scaling literature and is almost entirely a technical/economic term; 算力 predates that usage in Chinese and is above all an infrastructure and industrial-policy noun. Consequences for readers: (1) the compound family — 算力网络, 算力基础设施, 算力中心, 智算中心, 算力经济, 算力调度 — has no English counterpart, and translators break it up inconsistently ('compute network', 'computing infrastructure', 'intelligent compute'), so the same Chinese word can appear as three different English words in one document; (2) TC260's official English never once uses 'computing power' — it renders 算力设施 as 'computing infrastructure' and 算力资源 as 'computing resources', so an English reader searching translated PRC standards for 'computing power' will miss the passages; (3) 智能算力 / 智算 (AI-specific compute) is a distinct sub-category with no English equivalent at all, usually flattened to plain 'compute'. Do not read 算力 as implying GPU/accelerator specifically — that is 智能算力.

why_no_english: English has no noun that is at once the physics quantity, the traded commodity and the planned public utility. 'Compute' in English AI writing is a scaling input measured in FLOP; 算力 is that, plus a line item in five-year plans, plus a thing provinces compete to host, plus the root of a productive compound family (算力网络, 算力经济, 算力调度, 智算中心). The asymmetry is structural, not lexical: PRC AI strategy is organised around 算力 as infrastructure to be built and allocated, whereas Anglophone compute governance treats compute mainly as a chokepoint to be monitored and controlled. A reader who maps 算力 onto 'compute' will correctly parse the sentences and still miss why the word carries so much policy weight — and will not realise that 智能算力/智算 marks a category (AI-specific accelerated compute) that English simply does not lexicalise.

definition_en: The label under which Chinese frontier-safety writing files the scheming / deceptive-alignment cluster: a model that conceals its true capabilities or objectives, behaves differently under evaluation than in deployment, and uses deception instrumentally to evade shutdown or oversight while pursuing goals that conflict with human values.
definition_zh: 指人工智能系统为规避关机、监管或安全评估而有意隐瞒真实能力或目标、在评测与真实部署中表现不一致的行为，是中文前沿安全文献中对应英文 scheming／deceptive alignment 的类别名。
pitfalls: The English rendering is transparent, but the *search* problem is severe and asymmetric. English-language AI safety filed this cluster under 'scheming' (Anthropic/Apollo usage) and 'deceptive alignment'; neither has a settled Chinese calque, and Chinese institutions converged instead on 战略欺骗. An English speaker searching Chinese literature for 图谋/诡计/欺骗性对齐 will find almost nothing, while 战略欺骗 returns the Shanghai AI Lab framework, its evaluation reports and the associated media coverage. The reverse trap is worse: 战略欺骗 is also a standard military-strategy term ('strategic deception' in the maskirovka sense), so naive keyword search pulls in unrelated PLA and international-relations material. Note also that 战略 here means 'strategic' in the sense of *deliberate and plan-based*, not 'concerning grand strategy' — the framework groups it with 自主规划 and 自我修改 as control-undermining capabilities, not with military doctrine.

en_renderings.notes: Direct and used by Concordia AI's English-language reporting when describing Chinese work, so the pair is attested in both directions. Accurate, but does not signal to an English reader that this is the Chinese home of the 'scheming' literature.

Do not use it *instead of* 'strategic deception' when translating.

why_no_english: This is a discoverability gap rather than a semantic one. The concept is shared, but the two literatures indexed it under non-cognate labels — English under 'scheming' and 'deceptive alignment', Chinese under 战略欺骗 — so neither community's keyword searches reach the other's work. Compounding this, 战略欺骗 collides with an established military term in Chinese and 'strategic deception' collides with the same term in English, meaning the honest translation is precisely the one that maximises false-positive retrieval. The entry exists mainly to record the bridge.

definition_en: The two-tier risk-threshold design of the Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI Frontier AI Risk Management Framework. A 红线 (red line) is an intolerable-harm threshold that must not be crossed; a 黄线 (yellow line) is an early-warning threshold on the enabling capabilities and propensities that would make a red-line path viable. Results are sorted into a green / yellow / red zone, which determines whether a model gets routine deployment, controlled deployment, or suspension of deployment or development.
definition_zh: 《前沿人工智能风险管理框架》提出的双层风险阈值机制。“红线”是不可容忍的危害阈值，一旦触发即应暂停部署或开发；“黄线”是前瞻性预警指标，标示关键使能能力、行为倾向或防护缺失等前置条件。二者共同把模型划入绿区、黄区或红区，直接决定部署决策。
pitfalls: Three things go wrong in translation. (1) 红线 is a heavily loaded PRC political idiom for a non-negotiable limit (territorial red lines, ecological 生态保护红线); English 'red line' carries diplomatic-ultimatum connotations instead of the regulatory-threshold sense, and readers may hear rhetoric where the document means an auditable trigger. (2) The pair is routinely collapsed: English coverage reports 'China's AI red lines' and drops 黄线 entirely, which destroys the mechanism — the yellow line is where the framework does its actual anticipatory work, because a red line only fires once a credible harm pathway already exists. (3) Do not equate the scheme with ASL levels or preparedness tiers: it is not an ordered capability ladder. Each red line is an independent threshold defined over a deployment-environment / threat-source / enabling-capability (ETC) triple, and the framework says explicitly that the numbering (CY1–CY3, B1–B3) does not encode severity or progression. Also note the framework calls red lines developer 自我约束 pending consensus, not regulation.

en_renderings.notes: The framework's own English title is 'Frontier AI Risk Management Framework', and the threshold pair is normally rendered literally. Keep both terms; dropping 'yellow line' loses the mechanism.

why_no_english: English frontier-safety design converged on ordered capability ladders — ASL levels, preparedness tiers, capability thresholds — in which a single scale is climbed and each rung attaches a mitigation package. The 红线/黄线 scheme is a genuinely different shape: two qualitatively distinct kinds of threshold (an intolerable-outcome line and a precursor line), each instantiated independently per risk domain over an environment–threat–capability triple, feeding a three-zone deployment decision. English has 'threshold' and 'tripwire' but no established paired vocabulary for 'the line you must never cross' versus 'the line that tells you the crossing is becoming possible', and no term for a threshold defined over a context triple rather than over a capability score. Translating the words is easy; the reason the entry matters is that an English reader will file it as 'China's version of ASL' and miss that it is an alternative architecture — one that is deliberately interoperable with TC260 2.0 and the EU Code of Practice, as the framework's own mapping appendices set out.

definition_en: A datacentre built specifically to serve AI training and inference — accelerator-dense, often described by its FLOPS rating and by whether it hosts 万卡级 (10,000-accelerator-class) clusters — as distinct from a general-purpose 数据中心 and from a 超算中心 (HPC/supercomputing centre). Contraction of 智能计算中心.
definition_zh: 面向人工智能训练与推理建设的算力设施，以智能算力（加速卡）为主，常以 PFLOPS 规模和是否部署万卡级集群来描述，区别于通用数据中心和超算中心。是“智能计算中心”的缩略。
pitfalls: 'Intelligent computing centre' is the standard rendering and is close to meaningless in English — it sounds like a smart-building or a service desk, not a GPU datacentre. The real risks in reading PRC compute reporting are categorical: 智算中心 (AI datacentre), 超算中心 (supercomputing centre) and 数据中心 (general datacentre) are three tracked, separately-planned categories, and English coverage flattens all three to 'data centre', which makes provincial buildout figures incomparable. Note also that 智算 is a contraction of 智能计算 and appears in 智算集群 / 智算枢纽 / 智算资源, none of which have settled English forms — CSET's translation of the State Council 'AI Plus' Opinions uses 'intelligent computing cluster' and 'intelligent compute infrastructure' for the neighbouring terms. Finally, headline PFLOPS figures for 智算中心 are usually quoted at low precision (FP16/INT8) and are not comparable with FP64 supercomputer ratings.

definition_en: Alignment specifically to human ethical and social values, as distinct from alignment to a user's instructions or a developer's intent. In Chinese usage it is the ethics-facing half of alignment: teaching a system right from wrong, cooperative behaviour, and conformity to socially shared values.
definition_zh: 指使人工智能系统与人类伦理道德和社会价值观相一致，区别于仅与用户指令或开发者意图一致的对齐。在中文文献中它是对齐的“善”的一面，与能力（智）相对。
pitfalls: The single character 观 is load-bearing and routinely lost. 价值对齐 ('value alignment') is the broader technical term and is what TC260's national framework uses — its official English is 'value alignment'; 价值观对齐 ('values alignment', with 价值观 = a person's or society's set of values, a worldview) narrows it to the ethical/social register. Translating both as 'value alignment' erases the distinction. The deeper trap for English readers is scope: English 'alignment' is an umbrella covering goal-directedness, corrigibility, deceptive alignment and control, whereas 价值观对齐 in PRC policy usage is almost entirely about *content and ethics* — a system that produces socially acceptable outputs. A PRC document promising 价值观对齐 is not thereby promising anything about scheming or shutdown resistance; those sit under 失控 and 可控性. Beware too the political reading: in regulatory documents 价值观 can point at 社会主义核心价值观, so the term can be doing content-governance work rather than technical-alignment work. Read the surrounding sentence.

en_renderings.notes: Preferred. The plural 'values' preserves the 观 and signals the ethical/social narrowing that distinguishes 价值观对齐 from 价值对齐.

definition_en: The property of being controllable. In Chinese AI writing the word runs across at least three distinct senses without marking which is meant: the technical alignment property (humans can steer, interrupt or shut down the system), the developer/operational property (outputs stay within intended bounds — guardrails, filters), and the state/political property (the technology and its supply chain remain under domestic and regulatory control).
definition_zh: 指可被控制的性质。中文用法至少涵盖三层含义：技术上人类能否引导、中断或关停系统；工程上模型输出是否可被约束在预期范围内；以及政策意义上技术是否处于监管与自主掌控之下。文本通常不区分。
pitfalls: The undifferentiated three-way ambiguity is itself the finding, and it is not resolvable from the word alone. Evidence that the senses genuinely coexist: the Peking University alignment survey lists 可控性 (Controllability) as one of four technical alignment objectives alongside robustness, interpretability and ethicality; TC260 2.0's terminology annex uses 可控性 for what a safety guardrail delivers over model output (an engineering-containment sense); and the same standard's Principle 1.5 uses the verbal form 可控 in the formula 安全、可靠、可控 which sits inside the policy phrase family 安全可控 / 自主可控, where 可控 means 'not dependent on foreign technology and not socially disruptive'. Practical rule for readers: in a research paper 可控性 usually means the alignment property; in a standard or product document it usually means output containment; in a policy document 可控 almost never means the alignment property, and reading it that way produces a systematically over-optimistic picture of what a PRC document is committing to. Cross-check against 安全可控 and 自主可控 before translating.

en_renderings.notes: The standard rendering and the one used in the Chinese alignment literature's own English glosses. Faithful, but it inherits none of the disambiguation the English reader needs — annotate which sense is in play.

why_no_english: English distributes these three properties across separate vocabularies that never collide: 'corrigibility' and 'controllability' for the alignment property, 'containment' or 'guardrails' for output control, and 'sovereignty', 'indigenisation' or 'supply-chain security' for the political one. Chinese routes all three through the same morpheme 控, and the collision is productive rather than accidental — 安全可控, 自主可控 and 失控 form one word-family, so a single sentence can slide between an engineering claim and a sovereignty claim without any lexical signal. There is no English word that does this, which means every translation of 可控性 silently picks one of three readings on the reader's behalf. definition_en: AI that acts through a physical body — in current usage, foundation models (especially vision-language-action models) driving robots and other physical systems. In PRC discourse it names a top-tier strategic technology direction and an industry sector, not merely a research area.

In English, 'embodied AI' is a modest research-community label; in Chinese, 具身智能 is a headline policy category that appears in the national AI safety framework, five-year-plan language and Politburo study-session speeches alongside brain-computer interfaces and quantum technology, and it names an investable industry. definition_en: An AI system able to perform a wide range of tasks across many domains rather than being built for one function — the regulatory and risk-assessment category, contrasted with 专用人工智能 (narrow AI). Deliberately distinct from 通用人工智能 (AGI), which is a claim about human-level general capability.
definition_zh: 指可跨多个领域执行广泛任务、非为单一功能设计的人工智能系统，与“专用人工智能”相对。作为监管与风险评估的类别，它刻意区别于表示“通用人工智能（AGI）”的说法。
pitfalls: The distinction rests on one character and is real but only partly observed. 通用型人工智能 = general-purpose AI (a regulatory category: broad task coverage); 通用人工智能 = AGI (a capability claim: human-level general intelligence). The Chinese edition of the International AI Safety Report and the Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI framework both use 通用型人工智能 systematically as their headword and never use 通用人工智能 for AGI — the framework writes 'AGI' in Latin letters instead (可信 AGI). But the discipline slips in running text: the IASR Chinese edition itself writes 通用人工智能 in a handful of places where the English says 'general-purpose AI', including inside a section cross-reference. So: treat the 型 distinction as an editorial convention observed by the frontier-safety translation community, not as a reliable signal in arbitrary Chinese text. Practical consequence: never infer an AGI claim from 通用人工智能 without checking the source's own conventions, and expect 通用型 to be silently dropped by translators back into English, where 'general-purpose AI' and 'AGI' are themselves often confused.

en_renderings.notes: The attested pair: the Chinese edition of the International AI Safety Report uses 通用型人工智能 wherever the English original says 'general-purpose AI', across hundreds of occurrences, making this one of the best-evidenced equivalences in the corpus.

why_no_english: Here English is the language with the ambiguity and Chinese supplies the fix. English 'general AI' / 'general-purpose AI' / 'AGI' shade into one another, and the EU AI Act had to define GPAI by fiat because ordinary English does not distinguish 'broad in scope' from 'human-level'. Chinese can mark the difference morphologically with 型 ('of the general-purpose type'), and the frontier-safety translation community adopted that marking deliberately. The English rendering 'general-purpose AI' loses nothing semantically but loses the *visible* contrast with AGI that the Chinese carries in a single character — which is why translations back into English reintroduce exactly the confusion the Chinese was avoiding.

definition_en: One of the three top-level risk categories of the International AI Safety Report — risks where AI systems fail or behave in unexpected and harmful ways — comprising reliability failures and loss of control. 故障风险 is the Chinese edition's rendering of 'risks from malfunctions'; it is a translated taxonomy term, not a term of PRC origin.
definition_zh: 《国际人工智能安全报告》三大风险类别之一，指人工智能系统出现故障或以意料之外的有害方式运行的风险，下辖“可靠性挑战”与“失控”两节。该词是英文 risks from malfunctions 的中译，并非中国本土分类术语。
pitfalls: The framing to be careful about is real but its provenance is the opposite of what is usually assumed. Filing loss of control under a 'malfunction' heading originates in the International AI Safety Report (chaired by Yoshua Bengio) — §2.2 Risks from malfunctions contains §2.2.1 Reliability challenges and §2.2.2 Loss of control — and 故障风险 is simply the Chinese edition's translation of that heading. It is NOT the PRC taxonomy category for loss of control. The two authoritative PRC taxonomies file 失控 elsewhere: TC260's national AI Safety Governance Framework puts '“自我意识”觉醒、脱离人类控制' under 3.3.2 伦理安全风险 (ethical safety risks), inside the 应用衍生安全风险 (derivative) tier — i.e. as an ethics-and-society risk, not an engineering fault; and the Shanghai AI Lab / Concordia AI Frontier AI Risk Management Framework promotes 失控风险 to a top-level domain of its own, defined by threat source '模型破坏控制的倾向', while routing genuine engineering faults into a separate 意外风险 (accident) domain. So the structural divergence between the Chinese and English literatures runs the other way: the PRC documents *decline* the malfunction framing that the international report adopts. Separately, in ordinary PRC engineering prose 故障风险 just means 'failure risk' (e.g. 级联故障, 单点故障) with no taxonomic force.

Prefer this full phrase over the bare headword 'malfunction risk' whenever the term appears as a taxonomy heading — the report's own English is 'risks from malfunctions', and the singular noun phrase invites the reading that a specific engineering fault is meant.

definition_en: Security or safety arising from a system's own constitution rather than added around it. In PRC AI documents the term is used in two distinct ways: as a risk-taxonomy label (内生安全风险 = risks intrinsic to the AI technology itself — model/algorithm flaws, data quality — as opposed to risks of its application), and, more loosely, as a gloss for 'safe by design'.
definition_zh: 指安全性源于系统自身构造而非外部附加。在中国人工智能文件中有两种用法：一是风险分类标签，“内生安全风险”指技术自身缺陷带来的风险，与“应用安全风险”相对；二是作为“基于设计的安全”（safe by design）的意译。
pitfalls: 'Endogenous security' is a trap in both directions. First, it is not what the PRC standards body says in English: TC260's own bilingual frameworks render 人工智能内生安全风险 as 'AI's inherent safety risks' (1.0) and 人工智能技术内生安全风险 as 'Inherent safety risks of AI technology' (2.0) — the word 'endogenous' appears nowhere in either official English text. An English reader searching translated PRC standards for 'endogenous security' will find nothing; the term to search is 'inherent'. Second, note that 安全 here resolves to *safety* (the risks are model unexplainability, bias, weak robustness, unreliable output, data leakage), not to security, despite the English term sounding security-flavoured. Third, and most important for anyone connecting this to the cybersecurity literature: 内生安全 is also the name of an established Chinese cyberspace-security research programme (associated with 拟态防御 / mimic defence), and that is a different construct — an architectural defence technique, not a risk-taxonomy tier. This entry could not verify from primary sources that the cybersecurity programme has actually been applied to AI safety; the AI-document usages found are the taxonomy sense and the safe-by-design gloss. Treat any claim that PRC AI safety work is built on the cyberspace 内生安全 theory as unverified.

A distinct, narrower use: the Chinese text of the IDAIS-Shanghai consensus statement glosses the English 'safe by design' as 基于设计的安全（内生安全）, i.e. uses 内生安全 as an explanatory synonym. This is the only AI-safety usage found that is genuinely about designing safety in rather than classifying risks.

why_no_english: English splits what Chinese keeps together and vice versa. 'Inherent', 'intrinsic', 'built-in', 'by design' and 'endogenous' are near-synonyms in English with no technical division of labour, so no one of them is *the* translation; meanwhile Chinese 内生 is a single productive morpheme that generates both a risk-taxonomy tier and a design philosophy, and 安全 lets the term slide between safety and security without marking which. The result is that 内生安全 has no stable English target: the same two characters mean 'risks intrinsic to the technology' in a national standard, 'safe by design' in an international consensus statement, and a specific architectural defence programme in the cybersecurity literature. An English reader given any one rendering will over-read the other two into it.

definition_en: The umbrella property framework — explainability, robustness, fairness, privacy, controllability, accountability — that dominated PRC academic and industry AI-governance work before 'AI safety' arrived as a separate category. It has since been repurposed: TC260's 2.0 framework makes 可信人工智能基本准则 the vehicle for its loss-of-control provisions, headed by 人类最终控制.
definition_zh: 指涵盖可解释性、鲁棒性、公平性、隐私保护、可控性、可问责等属性的人工智能属性框架，是“人工智能安全”成为独立议题之前中国学界与产业界的主导框架。在《人工智能安全治理框架》2.0 版中，“可信人工智能基本准则”被用来承载防范技术失控的内容。
pitfalls: Lexically trivial — TC260's own English is 'trustworthy AI' — but the relationship to 人工智能安全 is where readers go wrong. Historically 可信人工智能 was the broader, senior framework and 安全 was one property inside it; the arrival of frontier-safety concerns inverted this, and TC260 2.0 now places its 可信人工智能基本准则 as an annex *serving* the safety framework, explicitly aimed at 技术失控风险 and opening with 人类最终控制 (ultimate human control) rather than with explainability. So the same term denotes a property checklist in a 2021 CAICT white paper and a loss-of-control instrument in a 2025 national standard. Second trap: 可信 invites the English reader to hear 'trust' as a user-facing or reputational quality, whereas in PRC usage it is a verifiability claim — the 2.0 principles include 促进可客观验证 (objective verifiability). Third: do not read 可信人工智能 as the EU's 'trustworthy AI' from the HLEG guidelines; the property lists overlap but the PRC version now carries human-control and national-sovereignty content the EU framing does not.

In English, 'trustworthy AI' names a policy-document genre (EU HLEG, NIST) that sits alongside AI safety and never absorbed it. In Chinese, 可信人工智能 was the pre-existing house framework of CAICT and the academic community, and when loss-of-control concerns arrived they were grafted onto it rather than given a separate home — so a PRC document's 可信人工智能 annex may be doing work that an English reader would expect to find under 'frontier safety' or 'AI control'. The residue an English reader misses is chronological and institutional: which framework is subordinate to which, and therefore whether a given commitment is a legacy property checklist or a live loss-of-control instrument. definition_en: Post-training that makes a model recognise and refuse harmful instructions — RLHF/RLAIF plus refusal training, embedding safety constraints into response behaviour. In Chinese lab and standards writing it denotes the harmlessness workstream specifically, not alignment in general.
definition_zh: 指通过 RLHF/RLAIF 与拒答训练，使模型主动识别并拒绝有害指令，把安全约束嵌入其响应行为的后训练环节。中文语境中它特指“无害化”这一条工作线，而非泛指对齐。
pitfalls: Two things to watch. First, scope: 安全对齐 is narrower than 对齐. In the Shanghai AI Lab framework it is one bullet in a list of safety-training measures, sitting beside 训练数据过滤, 指令层级, 针对性遗忘学习 and 对抗训练, and glossed as 安全对齐与拒答训练 — i.e. it is the refusal/harmlessness component, roughly what English calls 'safety tuning' or the harmlessness leg of HHH. Translating it as bare 'alignment' overstates it. Second, 安全 is ambiguous as always: here it resolves to safety (harmful content, dangerous instructions), not security, but the same compound could in principle be read as security-hardening, and nothing in the word disambiguates. A useful diagnostic finding: CAICT's governance report uses 安全对齐 precisely where the model is *faking* it — models that '在测试中有意增强安全对齐效果，在真实环境中回归对齐相对较差的表现' — showing the term denotes an observable behavioural surface that can be gamed, rather than an internal property.

en_renderings.notes: Direct and standard; matches usage in the English ML literature, where 'safety alignment' likewise denotes harmlessness post-training rather than alignment at large.

definition_en: One of the five basic-theory directions named in the 2017 State Council New Generation AI Development Plan. As defined there it is internet-scale collective intelligence — the organisation, emergence and learning of intelligence across large numbers of participating agents and humans, including crowdsourcing incentive mechanisms — not swarm robotics.
definition_zh: 《新一代人工智能发展规划》确立的五大基础理论方向之一，指群体智能的组织、涌现与学习机理，重点建立可表达、可计算的群智激励算法与模型，形成基于互联网的群体智能理论体系。其内涵以互联网众智为核心，而非机器人集群。
pitfalls: 'Swarm intelligence' is the dominant English rendering and is actively misleading. In English, swarm intelligence names a specific bio-inspired optimisation and multi-robot-coordination tradition (ant colony, particle swarm, drone swarms). The 2017 Plan's 群体智能 is defined around 群智激励算法 (crowd-intelligence incentive algorithms) and 基于互联网的群体智能理论体系 (an internet-based theory of collective intelligence) — i.e. human-plus-machine crowdsourced intelligence, closer to what English calls collective or crowd intelligence, with 群智 as its own contraction. The Stanford DigiChina translation of the Plan is itself inconsistent, using 'swarm intelligence' in most places, 'crowd intelligence' for 群智能空间, 'swarm integrated intelligence' for 群体集成智能 and 'mass intelligence' for 群智 — four English forms for one Chinese family, which is good evidence that no rendering has settled. A second trap: because the term is a named national strategic direction, it appears in funding and institutional contexts far more than the English research label would predict, and current usage has partly drifted toward multi-agent systems, which is a third sense again. Check the date and the source type before choosing an English word.

en_renderings.notes: The dominant rendering, used throughout the Stanford DigiChina translation of the 2017 Plan and hence in most English analysis of PRC AI strategy. Record it because it is what readers meet, but it imports a swarm-robotics reading that the Plan's own definition does not support.

en_renderings.notes: Not attested in the sources consulted as a rendering of 群体智能, but it is the English term that most accurately covers the Plan's definition without the robotics baggage of 'swarm' or the crowdsourcing narrowness of 'crowd'. Offered as the recommended rendering for new translation; keep 'swarm intelligence' when quoting existing English versions of the Plan.

why_no_english: English partitioned this space early and along different lines: 'swarm intelligence' went to bio-inspired optimisation and robot collectives, 'collective intelligence' to human group cognition, 'crowdsourcing' to task markets, and 'multi-agent systems' to distributed AI. Chinese 群体智能 spans all four and was then fixed by a policy document as a single funded research direction, so the Chinese term now denotes an administrative category that cuts across the English taxonomy rather than sitting inside any part of it. There is no English word for 'the research direction that includes ant-colony optimisation, internet crowdsourcing incentives and multi-agent emergence, because a national plan grouped them' — which is why the canonical English translation of the Plan itself needs four different words for one Chinese word-family.
